question: What natural-diet evidence does the 2004 Agusan Marsh gut-content study report, especially for dalag, tilapia and other familiar fishes, and can those observations be generalized or used as bait advice?

source.citation: Talde, C. M., Mamaril, A. C., Sr., & Palomares, M. L. D. (2004). The diet composition of some economically important fishes in the three floodplain lakes in Agusan Marsh wildlife sanctuary in the Philippines. Sri Lanka Journal of Aquatic Sciences, 9(1), 45-56. https://doi.org/10.4038/sljas.v9i1.7465
source.publisherMetadata: The publisher listing identifies the article as Open Access and says it is licensed under a Creative Commons License, but the captured listing does not specify the license version.
source.fullTextProvenance: The full text used for this research-only review was text-extracted from a SciSpace-hosted PDF mirror. The publisher page confirms the article metadata and open-access status, but the publisher-hosted PDF could not be retrieved in this pass; the mirror is not treated as an independent publisher record.
source.studyPeriodAsReported: Monthly sampling November 1998-December 1999; diet tables label the gut-content analysis November 1998-October 1999.
source.studyArea: Three floodplain lakes in the southeastern Agusan Marsh; the article describes access through the Agusan River.

methods.collectionAndAnalysis: Fish were captured using gillnets, long lines, hook-and-line, bamboo traps and scoop nets; the authors say traps and scoop nets were discontinued because they were used only along riverbanks. Gut samples were preserved after capture and examined in a laboratory. Identified food items were counted and quantified by volume; the article also reports frequency, number and volume components for a relative-importance index.
methods.baitBoundary: The article separately lists live bait used on long lines, including crabs, frogs, earthworms, snails, Trichogaster trichopterus and Puntius binotatus. Those are capture-method details, not automatically gut-content observations or bait recommendations.
methods.sampleSizeCaveat: The paper reports 578 guts overall but the reviewed tables do not provide a clear per-species, per-lake sample-size crosswalk for every diet observation.

observations.evidenceTable: Table 1, Present Study; discussion and Tables 2-3
gutContentsAsParaphrased: fish scales and other fish fragments
observations.localContext: The discussion specifically says fish from Ticgon and Dinagat contained substantial detritus. It also reports small Trichogaster trichopterus and Puntius binotatus among fish found in channid guts.
observations.interpretationLimit: Fish material supports fish consumption in this historical study, but the article does not report Channa striata as prey; it therefore does not establish cannibalism. The Table 1 food list is not fully resolved to lake, month, size class or individual stomach.

observations.evidenceTable: Table 1, Present Study; Table 2 pools the species across T, D and M
gutContentsAsParaphrased: detritus described by the authors as fine soil sediments
observations.localContext: The Table 2 site field is pooled across Ticgon, Dinagat and Mihaba rather than providing separate lake-specific rows for this taxon.
observations.interpretationLimit: The reviewed Present Study row does not list worms or insects; that omission is not proof they are never eaten. Do not substitute the article's separately labeled literature or interview column for measured local gut contents.

observations.localContext: The authors say the relative ordering of major foods differed among the three lakes.
observations.interpretationLimit: Do not merge the Present Study gut findings with separately listed literature, interview reports or the listed use of this fish as live bait.

observations.evidenceTable: Table 1, Present Study; Table 2 pools the species across T, D and M
observations.localContext: The article's discussion also names P. binotatus among small fish found in channid guts.
observations.interpretationLimit: Preserve the paper's name as printed until a separate taxonomic crosswalk is reviewed.

observations.evidenceTable: Table 1, Present Study; discussion and Table 2
observations.localContext: The authors describe detritus, phytoplankton and macrophytes as important components while reporting lake-to-lake differences in their relative ordering.
observations.interpretationLimit: The paper itself cautions that the importance of some animal items is unclear because the relative-importance results emphasize detritus and phytoplankton.

sourceScope.seasonality: The abstract reports generally larger gut-food volumes during flood months than during the dry season for several named fishes and increased empty stomach frequency in Channa striata as the dry season proceeded. This is a historical study pattern, not a current forecast.
sourceScope.evidenceColumns: Table 1 separates Present Study gut observations from Earlier Studies and Ethnobiological Survey. Only the Present Study observations were summarized above. The ethnobiological column is described as based on interviews with local residents/fishers and is not equivalent to examined stomach contents.

decision.reason: This is valuable direct gut-content evidence for three named historical floodplain lakes, but it is roughly 25 years old, has incomplete sample-to-site detail, contains internal sampling-period and place-name spelling variants, and has unverified current taxonomic mappings. The publisher's Creative Commons version is not specified in the captured metadata.

limitations: The study reflects fish collected in 1998-1999 in three lakes, not all Agusan Marsh waters, all Caraga waters or the whole Philippines.
The methods period runs to December 1999 while the diet tables are captioned November 1998 through October 1999.
Lake-name spellings vary in the article (Ticgon/Tigcon/Ticcon); no geometry or administrative crosswalk was inferred.
Food lists and relative-importance categories do not identify the prey species for every stomach; fish fragments do not identify conspecific prey.
Capture bait is reported separately and must not be treated as stomach-content evidence or fishing advice.
The article's literature and Indigenous Knowledge System interview columns remain distinct from current-study gut observations.
No item-specific permission for app republication or table reproduction was established; no article table, image or full-text copy is stored in the repository.
nextAction: Accepted-name crosswalk is recorded separately in national-caraga-agusan-marsh-talde-2004-taxonomy-crosswalk-20261031.json. Keep the paper's 2004 name strings and local evidence attached; diet information remains research-only pending item-level reuse and product-content review.
